introduction-beyond-simple-buckets.core: S3 is a regional object store with 11 nines of durability, effectively unlimited scale and a rich feature set: storage classes, lifecycle rules, versioning, replication, Object Lock, event notifications, access points and in-place querying. It underpins data lakes, backups, static sites and ML datasets.

first_principles.problem: Teams use S3 as a dumb file bucket and miss cost, security and data-management features.
truths: Objects are stored redundantly across AZs.
Access patterns vary over an object's life.
Buckets are often the target of data leaks.

analogy.title: A self-managing warehouse
analogy.story: It moves old boxes to cheaper back rooms, keeps copies, locks critical records and notifies you when deliveries arrive.
analogy.breaks: Warehouses have physical limits; S3 scales without capacity planning.

example.title: Secure bucket baseline
flow: Lifecycle to cheaper classes after 30 days
example.outcome: S3 used as a platform, not a folder.

check.q: What durability does S3 Standard target?

strong-consistency-the-read-after-write-.core: Since December 2020, S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all PUTs, DELETEs and LIST operations at no extra cost: after a successful write, any subsequent read or list returns the latest version. This removed a class of data-pipeline bugs caused by eventual consistency.

first_principles.problem: A Spark job lists a prefix right after writing and misses newly written files (pre-2020 behaviour).
truths: Distributed systems often trade consistency for performance.
derivation: Rely on **read-after-write** for new and overwritten objects.
Remember: concurrent writers still need **coordination** (last writer wins).

analogy.title: A shared notice board that updates instantly
analogy.story: Once you pin a notice, everyone who looks sees it.
analogy.breaks: Two people pinning at once see a clear order; S3 resolves concurrent writes as last-writer-wins, without locking.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No retries or consistency layers needed.

check.q: Does strong consistency make concurrent writers safe?
check.a: No: S3 applies last-writer-wins; use conditional writes or locking for coordination.

storage-classes-the-hierarchy-of-cost-vs.core: S3 classes trade storage price against retrieval cost and latency: Standard (hot), Intelligent-Tiering (automatic), Standard-IA and One Zone-IA (infrequent, retrieval fee), Glacier Instant Retrieval (ms access, archive price), Glacier Flexible Retrieval (minutes–hours) and Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, ~12 hours). Minimum durations and object sizes apply.

first_principles.problem: Petabytes of rarely read logs sit in Standard, costing far more than needed.
truths: Cheaper storage has retrieval costs and minimums.
derivation: **Glacier IR** for quarterly with ms access.
Mind **minimum duration** and **128 KB minimum** billing.

analogy.title: Storing belongings
analogy.story: Your desk, a cupboard, the loft and an off-site storage unit, each cheaper and slower to reach.
analogy.breaks: Your loft doesn't charge per retrieval; Glacier classes do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Moving cold logs to Deep Archive cuts storage ~95%.

check.q: When is Intelligent-Tiering the best choice?
check.a: When access patterns are unknown or changing, since it moves objects between tiers automatically.

lifecycle-policies-automating-the-flow.core: Lifecycle rules automatically transition objects between storage classes and expire them after set ages, filtered by prefix, tags or size. They also clean up noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads, which otherwise silently accumulate cost.

first_principles.problem: Old log versions and abandoned multipart uploads quietly double the bill.
derivation: **Transition** by age (e.g. IA at 30d, Glacier at 90d).

analogy.title: An automatic filing clerk
analogy.story: Moves files to archive after a month and shreds them after seven years, without being asked.
analogy.breaks: Clerks notice exceptions; lifecycle rules apply blindly, so test filters carefully.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Seven-year retention at a fraction of the cost.

check.a: Failed multipart uploads leave invisible parts that are billed until removed.

object-lock-worm-compliance-security.core: Object Lock makes object versions write-once-read-many for a retention period. Governance mode lets specially permitted users override it; Compliance mode can't be shortened or removed by anyone, including root. Legal holds lock indefinitely. It protects backups from ransomware and meets regulations like SEC 17a-4.

first_principles.problem: Attackers with admin credentials delete backups before encrypting production.
truths: Immutability must hold even against privileged users.
derivation: Enable **Object Lock** (requires versioning; set at bucket creation or later).
Use **Governance** for testing or overridable retention.

analogy.title: A time-locked bank vault
analogy.story: Once set, not even the bank manager can open it before the timer expires.
analogy.breaks: Vault timers can be drilled; Compliance mode can't be bypassed short of closing the AWS account.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Backups survive a full credential compromise for 35 days.

check.q: What's the difference between Governance and Compliance mode?
check.a: Governance can be bypassed by users with special permission; Compliance cannot be shortened or removed by anyone.

s3-select-vs-athena-querying-data-in-pla.core: Athena runs serverless SQL (Trino/Presto) over data in S3 using a Glue catalog, billed per TB scanned, and supports joins, aggregations and partitions. S3 Select filtered a single object with simple SQL but is no longer offered to new customers. Use columnar formats (Parquet), partitioning and compression to cut scanned bytes and cost.

first_principles.problem: Analysts download gigabytes of logs to filter a few rows locally.
truths: Moving data is slow and costly.
derivation: Use **Athena** for SQL across many objects.

analogy.title: Asking a librarian to find passages versus borrowing every book
analogy.story: The librarian reads in place and brings back only the lines you need.
analogy.breaks: Librarians are free; Athena bills by bytes read.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Scans one day's partition: MBs, not TBs.

code.text:
SELECT status, count(*)
FROM alb_logs
WHERE day = '2026-10-17' AND status >= 500
GROUP BY status;

check.q: Why does converting CSV to Parquet reduce Athena cost?
check.a: Parquet is columnar and compressed, so queries read only needed columns and far fewer bytes.

presigned-urls-the-temporary-guest-pass.core: A presigned URL embeds a signature from credentials that can access an object, letting anyone holding the URL GET or PUT that specific object until it expires, without AWS credentials or a public bucket. It enables direct browser uploads and secure downloads that bypass your servers.

first_principles.problem: Users upload large videos through the API servers, overloading them, or the bucket is made public for downloads.
derivation: Backend **generates** a URL for a specific key and method.
URL validity is capped by the **signer's credential lifetime**.

analogy.title: A single-use guest pass to one room
analogy.story: Valid for one door, one purpose, until it expires.
analogy.breaks: Guest passes are single-use; presigned URLs can be reused until expiry.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Browser uploads straight to S3 for 15 minutes.

code.text:
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client('s3')
url = s3.generate_presigned_url('put_object',
    Params={'Bucket': 'uploads', 'Key': f'users/{uid}/video.mp4', 'ContentType': 'video/mp4'},
    ExpiresIn=900)

check.q: Why can a presigned URL stop working before its expiry?
check.a: If it was signed with temporary credentials that expire first, the URL becomes invalid then.
